title: Reprocessing the Writing Process
author: Terry Heick and Nick Potkalitsky
source: Terry Heick's blog on Substack, February 9, 2026
summary: Heick and Potkalitsky reexamine the writing process, questioning whether the traditional stages (brainstorm, draft, revise, edit, publish) still serve student learning in an era of digital composition and AI. The classical process assumes linearity and finality; writers gather ideas, compose a first draft, receive feedback, and polish. But in practice, writers move nonlinearly: they revise as they go, jump between stages, and often discover their idea through the act of writing. Modern writing tools (Google Docs, collaborative editing, real-time feedback) have changed the work. And AI adds another layer: students can now collaborate with machines that suggest, generate, and expand ideas. The article argues for a reframed understanding of the writing process that honors nonlinearity, embraces AI as a thinking partner, and focuses feedback and instruction on the thinking that precedes and shapes writing. The authors propose a model that makes the invisible visible: prewriting, composition, feedback-integration, and revision are still present, but students should see them as recursive and interconnected, not sequential. The goal is not a perfect final product but a thinking trajectory—evidence of how the writer's understanding deepened. This shift makes AI use transparent and pedagogically sound: AI can assist with brainstorming, generate alternatives for consideration, or help articulate half-formed ideas. The learner's task is to evaluate, integrate, and refine what the tool produces. This is categorically different from using AI as a shortcut; it is leveraging AI to extend thinking.
points: The traditional linear writing process (brainstorm-draft-revise-edit-publish) no longer describes how writers actually work in digital environments.
Modern writers move nonlinearly, revising as they compose and discovering ideas through the act of writing rather than before it.
AI and collaborative tools have changed composition; the writing process should be reframed as recursive and interconnected stages rather than sequential.
Making thinking visible—showing the trajectory of how understanding deepened—is more important than a polished final product.

AI can assist writing instruction by serving as a thinking partner for brainstorming and idea development, provided students evaluate and refine its contributions rather than accepting them uncritically.
